heuristics.rule: Most tech PM H-1B petitions file under SOC 11-3021 (Computer and Information Systems Managers)
heuristics.condition: When an employer is filing an H-1B petition for a tech product manager role
heuristics.action: Use SOC 11-3021 as the occupational classification for prevailing wage determination and petition filing
heuristics.because: BLS and DOL classify most tech PM roles under SOC 11-3021; incorrect SOC code can affect prevailing wage level and petition validity
heuristics.regulatory_basis: BLS OOH SOC 11-3021; DOL Foreign Labor Certification Data Center

heuristics.rule: Under the wage-weighted H-1B lottery system effective February 2026, a PM at DOL Wage Level IV receives 4 lottery entries vs. 1 entry for Level I
heuristics.condition: When an H-1B petition for a PM is filed under SOC 11-3021 under the wage-weighted lottery system
heuristics.action: Assign the highest defensible DOL wage level to maximize lottery entries
heuristics.because: The wage-weighted H-1B system (effective February 2026) allocates lottery entries proportional to wage level: Level IV = 4 entries, Level I = 1 entry
heuristics.regulatory_basis: DOL wage-weighted H-1B lottery system, effective February 2026

heuristics.rule: BLS OEWS wage data captures base salary only and may undercount total compensation for tech PMs
heuristics.condition: When using BLS OEWS data to benchmark PM compensation for prevailing wage or offer evaluation purposes
heuristics.action: Supplement BLS data with industry surveys (levels.fyi, Glassdoor) for total compensation benchmarking
heuristics.because: RSUs and bonuses are a significant part of tech PM packages; BLS data does not capture these, potentially understating true market compensation by 1.5–2.5× at FAANG firms

heuristics.rule: BLS OEWS data is collected in May each year and published approximately 12–14 months later
heuristics.condition: When using BLS wage data for real-time compensation benchmarking
heuristics.action: Use BLS data for trend direction, geographic differentials, and occupational projections only — not for offer benchmarking
heuristics.because: May 2023 data was published March 2024; a 12–14 month lag makes it unsuitable for current offer-level precision

heuristics.rule: If a 'Senior PM' offer's total comp is below the levels.fyi median for that stated level, treat it as a signal that something is misrepresented before accepting.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an offer where the title says Senior PM but total comp is significantly below market median (e.g., $180K total vs. $350K+ median),
heuristics.action: ...verify the actual level code, not just the title, and determine whether the company has a sub-market comp culture or is back-loading equity in a way that reduces current value
heuristics.because: Title inflation is common; the level code and total comp structure reveal the true seniority and compensation band more accurately than the title alone

heuristics.rule: The 30–37 age range is the peak hirability window for senior IC and director PM roles in tech — treat it as a finite resource, not a baseline assumption.
heuristics.condition: When you are a PM in your early-to-mid 30s deciding whether to accelerate career moves or wait for organic progression...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize building credentials, network density, and optionality (founding, VC relationships, advisory roles) during this window rather than deferring those moves to your 40s
heuristics.because: EEOC data shows 40+ workers are structurally underrepresented in tech hiring relative to their workforce share, and the friction compounds after 40 — building optionality before the bias window closes is more effective than fighting it after

heuristics.rule: Model the US→Canada comp cut explicitly in dollar terms before accepting a Canadian role
heuristics.condition: When a US-based PM is considering a Canadian opportunity
heuristics.action: Convert both offers to USD using current exchange rate and compare total comp including equity, not just base salary
heuristics.because: A CAD $150K offer vs. a USD $200K offer looks closer than it is — it's actually a ~46% total comp reduction, which is easy to underestimate when comparing raw numbers

heuristics.rule: Use Amazon L5/L6 level codes as a translation layer when benchmarking across companies — Amazon L6 Senior PM is equivalent to Google/Meta Senior PM, not Amazon L5.
heuristics.condition: When comparing offers or leveling across Amazon and other major tech companies,
heuristics.action: ...map Amazon L6 to 'Senior PM' at Google/Meta rather than treating all 'PM' titles as equivalent
heuristics.because: Amazon's leveling nomenclature runs one step behind other companies; treating titles as equivalent without level-code mapping leads to systematic undervaluation or overestimation of seniority

heuristics.rule: If you are 40+ and job searching in tech, budget materially more time for the search — not because you are less qualified, but because the market friction is real and documented.
heuristics.condition: When a 40+ PM is planning a company switch and estimating how long the search will take...
heuristics.action: ...add significant buffer to timeline estimates and begin building pipeline earlier than a 30-year-old peer would need to
heuristics.because: Qualitative data shows 40+ job seekers face longer gaps between rounds, higher ghosting rates, and more 'culture fit' rejections — the friction is structural, not performance-based

heuristics.rule: Only accept a lateral Canadian role at a comp cut if Canadian PR is the explicit primary goal
heuristics.condition: When the Canadian role is the same seniority level as your current US role and comes with lower total comp
heuristics.action: Treat the comp reduction as the price of immigration security, not a career move
heuristics.because: A lateral move with a comp cut has no career upside to offset the financial loss unless immigration status is the actual objective

heuristics.rule: Treat signing bonus size ($50K–$150K at FAANG) as a proxy for how much unvested equity you are leaving behind at your current company.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether a signing bonus in a new offer is generous or merely standard,
heuristics.action: ...calculate your unvested equity cliff at current employer and compare it against the signing bonus being offered to determine if the switch is financially net-positive in year one
heuristics.because: Signing bonuses are structurally designed to cover unvested equity left behind; a mismatch means you are absorbing real financial loss that compounds over the vest schedule

heuristics.rule: For 40+ PMs, target enterprise tech, regulated industries, and non-consumer sectors rather than competing head-on in consumer tech IC markets.
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM over 40 is deciding which companies or sectors to target in a job search...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize fintech, healthtech, logistics, enterprise software (Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, Oracle), European-linked companies, and government/civic tech roles
heuristics.because: Age bias in tech hiring is concentrated in consumer tech IC roles — enterprise and regulated industries structurally value domain depth and customer relationships that take years to build, making experience an asset rather than a liability

heuristics.rule: At Canadian companies without recent funding rounds, treat equity as near-zero in your compensation calculation
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an offer from a Canadian-founded startup that is not publicly traded and has not recently raised a significant round
heuristics.action: Base your financial decision on base salary and bonus only; assign minimal value to equity
heuristics.because: Non-public Canadian companies' equity is illiquid with uncertain upside — it cannot be treated as equivalent to vested RSUs at US public companies

heuristics.rule: At FAANG, negotiate equity and signing bonus first — these are the most negotiable components and where the largest dollar variance occurs.
heuristics.condition: When entering compensation negotiation at a major tech company for a Senior PM role,
heuristics.action: ...anchor negotiation on RSU grant size and signing bonus rather than base salary, since base has a narrower band and equity/signing are where companies have more flexibility
heuristics.because: Base salary ranges are rigid and constrained by band; RSU grants and signing bonuses are deal-closing tools companies use with more discretion

heuristics.rule: Legal protection (ADEA) is not a practical career defense — network and credentials built before 40 are more effective than legal remedy after age discrimination occurs.
heuristics.condition: When a PM is weighing whether to rely on legal protections as a backstop against age discrimination...
heuristics.action: ...treat prevention through proactive credential-building and network investment as the primary strategy, not post-hoc legal action
heuristics.because: Proving age discrimination in a hiring decision is extremely difficult since companies don't document the reason, and EEOC processes are slow and typically result in settlements rather than systemic reform or job recovery

heuristics.rule: At Amazon Canada, do not evaluate the offer on Year 1 compensation
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an Amazon Canada PM offer
heuristics.action: Model total comp across all 4 years of the RSU vesting schedule, weighting Years 3–4 heavily
heuristics.because: Amazon's compensation is front-loaded with RSUs on an uneven vesting schedule — Year 1 is the lowest total comp year and misrepresents the actual package value

heuristics.rule: Non-FAANG Principal PM comp can match FAANG Senior PM comp — do not automatically assume FAANG is the only path to top-quartile compensation.
heuristics.condition: When a Senior PM is evaluating whether to join or stay at a non-FAANG company like Intuit versus pursuing a FAANG role,
heuristics.action: ...compare total comp at the target level (e.g., Principal PM at Intuit ~$482K) directly against FAANG Senior PM benchmarks (~$528K at Google L5) before assuming FAANG is materially better
heuristics.because: At senior individual contributor levels, well-compensated non-FAANG companies are competitive with FAANG; the prestige premium does not always translate to a compensation premium

heuristics.rule: The 'overqualified' signal in hiring feedback is a proxy for 'we think you'll leave or cost too much' — not a compliment and not a negotiable objection.
heuristics.condition: When a 40+ PM receives 'overqualified' feedback after an interview process...
heuristics.action: ...treat it as a strong signal to redirect search toward management track roles, advisory, or consulting rather than re-applying to IC-heavy organizations
heuristics.because: Overqualified is a documented pattern in how age discrimination surfaces in feedback — it bundles cost, tenure, and authority concerns into a single neutral-sounding phrase that is unlikely to resolve through negotiation

heuristics.rule: To close the Canada–US comp gap without relocating, target Principal PM or Director level at a major Canadian employer
heuristics.condition: When a Canadian-based PM is evaluating whether the comp gap justifies relocating to the US
heuristics.action: Assess whether a realistic level progression to Principal or Director in Canada would close the gap relative to mid-level US roles before deciding to relocate
heuristics.because: A Principal PM or Director in Canada at a major employer can reach CAD $220,000–$280,000, which is competitive with non-FAANG mid-level US roles when quality of life and immigration security are factored in

heuristics.rule: If your goal includes founding, VC, or pivot roles, pursue them before 40 — not because they become impossible after, but because institutional bias creates compounding friction the later you wait.
heuristics.condition: When a PM in their mid-30s is deciding whether to pursue a non-linear career move now versus waiting until they feel 'ready'...
heuristics.action: ...weight the time cost of waiting against the market friction that accrues after 40, and bias toward earlier action if optionality is the goal
heuristics.because: The data shows consumer tech structurally over-hires 25–35-year-olds, and the PM→VC, PM→advisory, PM→consulting pivots face less age discrimination than direct PM hiring — but building the network and credentials for those pivots still benefits from earlier investment

heuristics.rule: If you are on PGWP, treat your job search as open-market; do not self-filter for LMIA-sponsoring employers
heuristics.condition: When a PM candidate is on PGWP and job searching in Canada...
heuristics.action: ...apply to any Canadian employer including startups and mid-size companies that do not sponsor LMIA, because PGWP is employer-unrestricted
heuristics.because: PGWP requires no LMIA and is open work authorization, so self-filtering to large LMIA sponsors artificially shrinks the candidate pool and wastes competitive advantage

heuristics.rule: If mentoring energizes you but structured people development drains you, you are an IC, not a manager
heuristics.condition: When a Senior PM is deciding between IC and management tracks...
heuristics.action: ...distinguish between informal mentoring (IC-compatible) and systematic career development of direct reports (management-required) and assess which feels energizing vs. draining
heuristics.because: The management track allocates 30% of weekly time to 1:1 coaching and 25% to hiring — if those activities feel like a tax rather than a reward, the role will be miserable regardless of comp or title

heuristics.rule: If you're already at FAANG or top-tier tech, an MBA returns you to where you started at massive cost
heuristics.condition: When a Senior PM at a top-tier tech company considers an MBA to advance their career...
heuristics.action: ...do not pursue an MBA unless targeting a non-CPO-track role (e.g., strategy, GM, COO) where MBA is structurally expected
heuristics.because: MBA recruiting pipelines are designed to get candidates into companies like the one you already work at — the credential adds nothing to your existing access

heuristics.rule: Complete foundational work before leaving a PM role to found a company
heuristics.condition: When considering a PM-to-founder pivot...
heuristics.action: ...solve value proposition, cash burn estimate, and founding team identification before resigning
heuristics.because: Leaving without these solved means burning personal runway on problems that could have been de-risked while still earning a salary

heuristics.rule: Get the level code, not just the title
heuristics.condition: When evaluating any PM offer across companies...
heuristics.action: ...ask for the numeric or alphanumeric level code (L5, IC5, ICT4) and cross-reference it against the company's internal leveling structure before comparing to your current role
heuristics.because: Titles like 'Senior PM' are internally defined and not portable — the same title can represent radically different scope and compensation across companies

heuristics.rule: Subtract equity entirely and assess whether remaining compensation meets living expenses before accepting a startup offer.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a startup offer with significant equity as part of the compensation pitch...
heuristics.action: ...remove equity from the calculation entirely and evaluate whether base salary alone covers your financial needs
heuristics.because: ~90% of startups fail, dilution can reduce a 1% stake to 0.3%, liquidation preferences reduce payouts by 60–80%, and options often cost 20–50% of annual salary to exercise — making equity unreliable as income

heuristics.rule: If performance reviews are strong but promotions consistently go to people with political capital, you're hitting an org ceiling, not a skill gap
heuristics.condition: When you have strong reviews for multiple cycles but aren't advancing
heuristics.action: Diagnose whether the block is internal (skill) or structural (org), then act accordingly — fix skills or leave
heuristics.because: Skill gaps and org ceilings feel identical from the inside but require completely opposite responses; misdiagnosing wastes years

heuristics.rule: Target 8/10 job satisfaction as your navigation metric, not 10/10 or 5/10
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether to stay, push for change, or leave a role
heuristics.action: Rate your satisfaction on a 1-10 scale regularly and track it over time; act if it drops below 7 for six months, act urgently if below 5 for three months
heuristics.because: 10/10 is unrealistic and causes paralysis; 5/10 means you're enduring rather than building; 8/10 means you're engaged, growing, and pulling others upward

heuristics.rule: Expand scope first, demonstrate impact at that scope, then ask for the title
heuristics.condition: When pursuing promotion to the next level...
heuristics.action: ...seek expanded responsibilities before the title change, not after
heuristics.because: Promotions depend on demonstrated impact at higher scope, not mastery of a competency rubric — the title follows proof, not preparation

heuristics.rule: Block calendar time explicitly for strategic work — it will always lose to reactive work if unprotected
heuristics.condition: When you are a PM trying to develop or demonstrate senior-level strategic thinking...
heuristics.action: ...schedule dedicated, recurring calendar blocks for strategy development before your week fills with execution tasks
heuristics.because: Strategic work is non-urgent but high-importance; reactive work is always urgent and will crowd it out without structural protection

heuristics.rule: If you've been passed over multiple cycles with the same feedback, the org may not have structural room for you — not a skill gap
heuristics.condition: When you've received consistent positive reviews but repeated promotion denials with recycled feedback...
heuristics.action: ...treat this as an organizational ceiling signal and seriously evaluate an external move
heuristics.because: Repeated cycles with identical feedback without promotion usually indicates headcount, budget, or political constraints — not genuine development needs

heuristics.rule: Invest in communication skills disproportionately relative to how much of your job they represent
heuristics.condition: When deciding where to invest career development time as a senior PM
heuristics.action: Prioritize writing, speaking, and presenting skills even though they constitute a small fraction of daily work
heuristics.because: Presentations are 5% of the job but 50% of how you are judged — the return on communication investment is asymmetrically high relative to time spent

heuristics.rule: Target 12 continuous months in a NOC TEER 1 PM role immediately after receiving PGWP
heuristics.condition: When a PM on PGWP wants to maximize PR optionality via Express Entry...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize securing a qualifying PM role quickly and tracking 12-month clock from day one of employment
heuristics.because: 12 months of TEER 1 experience unlocks Canadian Experience Class eligibility, which is the most reliable PR pathway for international graduates without requiring LMIA or employer sponsorship

heuristics.rule: Try IC first if uncertain; do not try management first if uncertain
heuristics.condition: When a Senior PM is undecided between tracks in their 30s or earlier...
heuristics.action: ...default to IC track and keep the management option open rather than defaulting to management
heuristics.because: Transitioning IC → Management is easier than Management → IC; after 10+ years on the IC track, moving to management is difficult, but the reverse transition — from years of management back to IC — often requires accepting a lower-scope IC role

heuristics.rule: Name specific doors before committing — if you can't list them, the opportunity cost is too high
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether an MBA is worth the investment...
heuristics.action: ...identify by name the companies, roles, or recruiting funnels that are currently closed to you and would open with an MBA
heuristics.because: Vague rationales like 'I want to learn strategy' don't justify $400K–$500K in total opportunity cost; concrete, named access gaps do

heuristics.rule: Direct SPM-to-VC is rare; most successful PM-to-VC transitions go through VP/CPO or a founding stint first
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM is targeting VC as a next move...
heuristics.action: ...plan for an intermediate step (VP Product, founding, EIR) rather than applying directly to partner roles
heuristics.because: The career examples that succeeded all included operating leadership or founding experience before VC entry

heuristics.rule: Use compensation as a level verification signal
heuristics.condition: When a company states a title but the total comp offer seems off...
heuristics.action: ...check levels.fyi to verify the offer aligns with the median total comp for that stated level at that specific company
heuristics.because: If comp is below median for the stated level, the company may be soft-downleveling you while maintaining a flattering title

heuristics.rule: Evaluate a role by three questions — what will you own, what decisions will you make, and who will you influence — not by title.
heuristics.condition: When comparing offers with different titles or trying to assess the real scope of a role...
heuristics.action: ...replace title comparison with a structured assessment of decision surface, autonomy, and organizational reach
heuristics.because: Startups inflate titles because they can't compete on comp, and Big Tech has so many leveling bands that 'Senior' means wildly different things across orgs — title is a noisy signal

heuristics.rule: If you've solved the problems you were hired to solve and no new scope is available, it's time to leave
heuristics.condition: When internal growth path is genuinely exhausted — not just 'not this cycle'
heuristics.action: Switch companies rather than wait for scope that isn't coming
heuristics.because: Staying in a role with no new scope stalls your learning rate regardless of title or compensation

heuristics.rule: Test career hypotheses through small experiments before making full moves
heuristics.condition: When considering a domain change, company switch, or new role type
heuristics.action: Take on side projects, do informational interviews, or volunteer for cross-functional work before committing
heuristics.because: This gathers real data about fit and interest with low downside risk, converting anxious hope into actionable information

heuristics.rule: Make your judgment visible by explicitly unpacking your decision-making process
heuristics.condition: When operating at senior PM level where trust is required for expanded influence...
heuristics.action: ...articulate the alternatives you considered and why you chose a specific path, rather than just presenting conclusions
heuristics.because: Judgment is invisible unless you show your work — executives cannot calibrate trust in someone whose reasoning they cannot observe

heuristics.rule: Use the autonomy template when raising challenges to your manager: state the problem, state your proposed approach, ask for input
heuristics.condition: When you encounter a challenge or decision point and need to communicate upward...
heuristics.action: ...frame the conversation as: 'Here's the challenge, here's my proposed approach, any thoughts?' rather than presenting the problem alone
heuristics.because: This format signals decision-making capability and independent thinking while still inviting feedback — it demonstrates senior-level autonomy without bypassing collaboration

heuristics.rule: Own scope before the title, not after
heuristics.condition: When you want to demonstrate readiness for the next level...
heuristics.action: ...identify scope you can credibly take on and start owning it without waiting to be asked
heuristics.because: Promotions reward demonstrated performance at the next level, not potential — you have to show the work before the recognition

heuristics.rule: Separate title, money, and scope when evaluating any role or promotion
heuristics.condition: When assessing a new opportunity or a promotion offer
heuristics.action: Explicitly evaluate scope (decision authority and surface area) as the primary variable, treating title and money as secondary
heuristics.because: Title and money are legible and emotionally salient but scope is the strongest predictor of long-term career development; conflating them leads to underweighting the variable that actually matters

heuristics.rule: If you are a US-based PM at a company with Canadian offices, use ICT transfer rather than LMIA to enter Canada
heuristics.condition: When a US-based PM wants to relocate to Canada and their employer has Canadian operations...
heuristics.action: ...pursue Intra-Company Transfer (C-12 exemption) instead of triggering LMIA process
heuristics.because: ICT is LMIA-exempt and avoids 2–5 month LMIA wait, making employment start immediate and reducing employer friction

heuristics.rule: Use the diagnostic question: 'Do you want to be evaluated on your own product judgment, or on the quality of product judgment you develop in others?'
heuristics.condition: When a Senior PM cannot resolve the IC vs. management decision through self-assessment alone...
heuristics.action: ...answer this single question honestly, as it cuts through surface preferences to the core motivational difference between the two paths
heuristics.because: The two tracks have fundamentally different success criteria — IC success is personal expertise, management success is team output — and this question forces clarity on which success metric actually motivates the person

heuristics.rule: For PM specifically, specialized dual-degree programs outperform raw prestige rankings
heuristics.condition: When choosing between MBA programs with the goal of entering product management...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize programs with design/tech integration (e.g., Kellogg MMM) over higher-ranked generalist programs
heuristics.because: Kellogg MMM places 35% of graduates into PM vs. 8% for standard Kellogg MBA — program design matters more than brand rank for this specific outcome

heuristics.rule: Build pivot optionality before you need it, not after burnout hits
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM is still employed and performing well...
heuristics.action: ...invest in thought leadership, target-domain networking, and advisory roles now
heuristics.because: The best leverage for a pivot comes from a position of strength; burned-out job-seeking signals desperation and narrows options

heuristics.rule: Ignore startup titles entirely; ask about decision rights instead
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a startup offer with an elevated title (Director, VP)...
heuristics.action: ...ask 'What decisions can I make unilaterally? Who has override authority over the roadmap?' and map the answer to an equivalent FAANG scope level
heuristics.because: Startups use inflated titles as compensation substitutes for cash; the title signals nothing reliable about actual scope or organizational influence

heuristics.rule: Optimize for your next two jobs, not your entire career or just this year's salary.
heuristics.condition: When making a startup vs. Big Tech decision at any career stage...
heuristics.action: ...evaluate how this role positions you for the role after the next one, not just immediate compensation or prestige
heuristics.because: Neither path is wrong if you commit fully, but the sequencing and downstream optionality matter more than any single job's immediate rewards

heuristics.rule: Optimize for scope over title at every career stage
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a role or promotion offer
heuristics.action: Ask 'what's the most important decision I'll make in the next 12 months?' before accepting; walk away if the answer isn't immediately interesting
heuristics.because: Title without scope is a career trap — it looks good externally but doesn't build the skills that make you genuinely senior in the market sense

heuristics.rule: Make specific, concrete asks when reaching out to potential mentors
heuristics.condition: When seeking guidance from someone ahead of you in your target trajectory
heuristics.action: Ask a bounded, answerable question like 'Can we talk for 30 minutes about how you decided to move from X to Y?' instead of 'Can you be my mentor?'
heuristics.because: Generic asks get ignored; specific asks are easy to say yes to and demonstrate you've done your homework

heuristics.rule: Connect your work to company strategy explicitly, never assume the link is obvious
heuristics.condition: When presenting plans or requesting resources at senior levels...
heuristics.action: ...articulate why your area matters at the company level in every significant communication
heuristics.because: A senior PM who cannot explain their area's strategic relevance will be overlooked in resource allocation, regardless of execution quality

heuristics.rule: Articulate the conditional logic behind 'it depends' answers explicitly to demonstrate senior reasoning
heuristics.condition: When facing a complex decision where no single answer is obviously correct...
heuristics.action: ...identify and state the conditions: 'If X is true, then A is best; if Y is true, then B is best'
heuristics.because: The ability to articulate what makes an answer context-dependent is itself a senior-level skill — it shows systematic thinking rather than uncertainty or avoidance

heuristics.rule: Make your impact legible, not just real
heuristics.condition: When you've delivered meaningful business outcomes...
heuristics.action: ...actively surface and communicate those wins to your manager rather than assuming visibility
heuristics.because: Managers are overloaded and promotion decisions are made on available evidence — undocumented impact doesn't exist in calibration rooms

heuristics.rule: Partner with your manager by asking what gap exists between where you are now and the next level
heuristics.condition: When pursuing promotion
heuristics.action: Initiate a collaborative conversation with your manager that frames them as an ally with a role in your growth rather than a gatekeeper to negotiate against
heuristics.because: It transforms an adversarial dynamic into a collaborative one, gives your manager a clear role, and generates specific actionable feedback rather than vague hope

heuristics.rule: For Indian or Chinese nationals, plan a 3-year horizon to Canadian citizenship before the Canada → US TN pathway becomes viable
heuristics.condition: When an Indian or Chinese national is building a Canada → US career path and expecting to use TN visa...
heuristics.action: ...factor in Canadian citizenship timeline (3 years of PR) before the TN option unlocks, and evaluate H-1B or EB-1A alternatives in parallel
heuristics.because: TN visa is only available to Canadian and Mexican citizens, not PR holders of non-North American nationality, making the timeline significantly longer for this group

heuristics.rule: At Director level, choose track on fit not comp; at VP+ level, factor in comp ceiling if it matters
heuristics.condition: When a PM is using compensation as a primary decision driver...
heuristics.action: ...recognize that IC and management comp are comparable through Director level (~$315K vs. ~$370K), but management track has a meaningfully higher ceiling at VP+ ($405K+ vs. $380–$450K IC, with CPO reaching $480K–$750K+)
heuristics.because: Optimizing for comp at the Director fork is premature — the real comp divergence only appears at VP and above, and most people never reach that level

heuristics.rule: For a finance professional at $150K trying to enter PM, the MBA ROI math can work; for a Senior PM earning $250K+ at FAANG, it almost certainly doesn't
heuristics.condition: When running ROI analysis on an MBA...
heuristics.action: ...calculate whether the MBA increases total comp by more than $500K over your remaining career given your current trajectory
heuristics.because: The break-even threshold is whether the credential opens a comp bracket your current path doesn't reach — this is true for career switchers but rarely true for established PMs

heuristics.rule: Use a transitional role (EIR, CoS, advisory board) to bridge if a direct pivot is not yet credible
heuristics.condition: When a PM lacks the network or credentials for a direct entry into VC, founding, or C-suite...
heuristics.action: ...pursue a 12–24 month bridge role that provides the missing exposure or signal
heuristics.because: Transitional roles compress the credibility gap without requiring a full leap into an unfamiliar domain

heuristics.rule: A promotion without scope increase is a title bump, not a career move
heuristics.condition: When receiving an internal promotion where the new level has the same scope as the current role...
heuristics.action: ...treat it as a lateral and evaluate whether it creates overleveling risk for future external moves
heuristics.because: An elevated title without expanded scope can make you look overleveled to future hiring managers who will ask about actual scope, not titles

heuristics.rule: If you want both startup and Big Tech experience, do Big Tech first.
heuristics.condition: When early in your career and uncertain about sequencing startup vs. Big Tech...
heuristics.action: ...start at Big Tech to preserve optionality in both directions
heuristics.because: Big Tech → startup is easy and always available; startup → Big Tech requires either startup success or strong prior credentials, meaning starting at a startup narrows Big Tech entry options

heuristics.rule: If you can't list three genuinely hard problems you worked on in the last 12 months, your current role isn't developing you
heuristics.condition: When assessing whether to stay or leave a role
heuristics.action: Treat the inability to list three hard problems as a stronger signal than your performance review score
heuristics.because: Performance reviews measure past output; the hardness of your problems predicts future growth rate

heuristics.rule: Build relationships during good times, not when you need something
heuristics.condition: When your career is stable and you don't have an immediate need
heuristics.action: Stay in touch with your network proactively, without an agenda
heuristics.because: The people you maintained contact with when you didn't need anything are the ones who will go out of their way to help you later

heuristics.rule: Treat cross-stage transitions as fundamentally different jobs, not faster execution of the current job
heuristics.condition: When moving from PM2 to Senior PM, or from Senior PM to Director...
heuristics.action: ...deliberately shift focus to the new stage's responsibilities even if it means appearing temporarily less competent
heuristics.because: Cross-stage promotions require different work, not better work — attempting to get promoted by excelling at Stage 1 work will not unlock Stage 2 advancement

heuristics.rule: Accelerate the PM-to-Senior PM transition before any other career move — it has the greatest compounding effect
heuristics.condition: When prioritizing which career milestone to focus on...
heuristics.action: ...concentrate energy on clearing the Senior IC threshold first, ahead of pursuing management or director paths
heuristics.because: The first transition (PM to Senior PM, median 3 years) sets the pace for all subsequent milestones; accelerating it compresses the entire career timeline

heuristics.rule: Track named skill gaps monthly in a shared doc with your manager
heuristics.condition: When you've identified 2–3 specific limiting skills holding back your promotion...
heuristics.action: ...create a shared tracking document with your manager, naming each gap precisely, defining what 'fixed' looks like, and reviewing progress monthly
heuristics.because: Visible, documented progress removes ambiguity about what's needed and makes it harder to be passed over without a clear, specific explanation

heuristics.rule: Make your impact visible to decision-makers without relying on visibility happening organically
heuristics.condition: When you do high-impact work that is invisible (infrastructure, coordination, quality) or when you are a non-native English speaker or introvert
heuristics.action: Actively narrate your work and contributions to the people who need to see them
heuristics.because: Promotion committees suffer from presentation bias and will judge on high-visibility moments; if your work is invisible, you are systematically disadvantaged regardless of actual impact

heuristics.rule: Use Canada as a base for early-career PM experience and immigration security; plan US transition for mid-career scope maximization
heuristics.condition: When an ambitious PM is deciding whether to build their career in Canada or US long-term...
heuristics.action: ...treat Canada as a 2–4 year strategic platform for securing immigration status and building foundational experience, then evaluate US transition for principal/director-level scope
heuristics.because: Canadian PM experience is respected but Canadian market size structurally limits product scope and total comp relative to US; early career benefits outweigh later-career ceiling

heuristics.rule: If a PM's primary identity is domain expertise, route them toward IC; if it is team building, route them toward management
heuristics.condition: When assessing track fit for a Senior PM...
heuristics.action: ...ask what they would want to be known for in 10 years — being the expert on the hardest problems, or having developed a generation of strong PMs
heuristics.because: Principal ICs spend 40% of time on deep product strategy and build domain expertise as their primary value; Directors spend only 15% on product strategy and derive value from team output, not personal expertise

heuristics.rule: Post-2022, treat MBA→PM as a harder path than historical data suggests
heuristics.condition: When using pre-2022 placement rates to forecast MBA ROI for PM roles...
heuristics.action: ...discount those figures and research 2023–2024 actual placement rates, accounting for tech layoffs and reduced MBA intake at major tech companies
heuristics.because: Amazon paused MBA hiring, Google cut headcount, Meta/Microsoft reduced MBA intake post-2022; nearly 25% of HBS Class of 2024 was still job-searching 3 months post-graduation

heuristics.rule: EIR roles require demonstrated 0-to-1 product creation, not just scaled-product experience
heuristics.condition: When a PM is evaluating EIR eligibility...
heuristics.action: ...assess whether their track record includes building totally new products from scratch, not just scaling existing ones
heuristics.because: VC firms place EIRs to identify and build new companies; scaled-product experience does not validate this specific capability

heuristics.rule: Amazon L-numbers run one level inflated relative to FAANG peers
heuristics.condition: When comparing Amazon PM levels to Google or Meta...
heuristics.action: ...subtract one level from Amazon's code to find the scope equivalent (Amazon L6 ≈ Google L5 ≈ Meta IC5)
heuristics.because: Amazon's L-scale is inflated relative to peer companies, so direct number comparisons create false equivalencies

heuristics.rule: Early career (0–5 years): prioritize learning velocity over everything else, including compensation.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating offers in the first five years of a PM career...
heuristics.action: ...weight learning speed and breadth of exposure above salary, title, or brand name
heuristics.because: Startup experience at a failed company with meaningful scope still teaches more than 2 years as a mid-level PM in a large Big Tech team — the compound returns on early learning outweigh short-term comp differences

heuristics.rule: If your manager can't describe what the next level looks like and name two people who got there, there is no defined path
heuristics.condition: When evaluating internal promotion prospects
heuristics.action: Don't wait for a promotion cycle — confirm the path is real before investing in it
heuristics.because: Without a defined and evidenced path, advocacy is impossible and the goalposts will move

heuristics.rule: Treat a persistent feeling of incompetence as a signal of high learning, not failure
heuristics.condition: When you've taken on a new role or domain and feel out of your depth
heuristics.action: Stay the course and treat the discomfort as the cost of growth rather than a sign you made the wrong move
heuristics.because: If you're always competent, you're not growing; the steepest learning curves coincide with the highest periods of development

heuristics.rule: Use 360-degree feedback as a proxy for collaborative reputation before seeking scope expansion
heuristics.condition: When assessing readiness for senior-level expanded influence...
heuristics.action: ...solicit feedback on whether peers and stakeholders view you as constructive, humble, and genuinely collaborative
heuristics.because: Executives pattern-match heavily on collaboration signals when deciding who gets expanded scope — defensive or self-interested reputations block advancement regardless of output quality

heuristics.rule: Answer 'why?' for every roadmap component to transform a timeline into a strategic framework
heuristics.condition: When building a product roadmap...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly document the reasoning behind each item, not just what will be built and when
heuristics.because: A roadmap without 'why' is a schedule; a roadmap with 'why' is a strategy — the latter signals senior-level ownership of direction, not just execution

heuristics.rule: Identify who has calibration-level influence, not just your direct manager
heuristics.condition: When building relationships to support your promotion...
heuristics.action: ...find and cultivate a real relationship with someone who has actual influence in the calibration process, not just your direct manager
heuristics.because: Promotion decisions happen in rooms you're not in — a well-intentioned but low-influence advocate cannot move the needle regardless of what they say

heuristics.rule: Build peer relationships and coaching circles during good times, not when you need them
heuristics.condition: When your career is stable and you are not actively job searching or navigating a crisis
heuristics.action: Invest time in building peer networks proactively
heuristics.because: By the time you need a network for a job search or difficult situation, it is too late to build it — relationships built under no pressure are far more useful than ones built under urgency

heuristics.rule: Publish market teardowns and investment theses publicly to position for VC
heuristics.condition: When targeting a VC pivot...
heuristics.action: ...write up investment analyses on real companies and distribute them before applying to any firm
heuristics.because: VCs assess analytical thinking and point-of-view credibility; published work demonstrates both in a way a resume cannot

heuristics.rule: Validate a downlevel by requiring a defined upgrade path with a stated timeline
heuristics.condition: When considering accepting a lower title at a target company...
heuristics.action: ...only accept if the company provides explicit promotion criteria and a typical time-to-promo for moving to the next level
heuristics.because: Without a stated upgrade path, a downlevel at a prestigious company may become a permanent level reset rather than a temporary step

heuristics.rule: Set a 1-week information-gathering deadline, then decide and commit.
heuristics.condition: When stuck in prolonged deliberation between startup and Big Tech offers...
heuristics.action: ...time-box due diligence to one week, then make a full commitment
heuristics.because: Half-hearted commitment produces poor outcomes in either environment — the quality of execution after the decision matters more than marginal improvement in the decision itself

heuristics.rule: If you're not in strategy-setting conversations after 18 months, ask why before concluding it's an org ceiling
heuristics.condition: When you feel excluded from key organizational decisions
heuristics.action: Diagnose whether exclusion reflects thin stakeholder relationships (fixable) or a structural org ceiling (leave)
heuristics.because: Mistaking thin relationships for an org ceiling causes PMs to leave problems they could have solved

heuristics.rule: At each career stage transition, identify what you were good at that you now need to stop doing
heuristics.condition: When moving from Senior PM to Director/VP or any stage-level promotion
heuristics.action: Explicitly inventory the hands-on behaviors that made you successful and create a plan to delegate or deprioritize them
heuristics.because: The VP who keeps trying to be a great Senior PM will fail as a VP; stage transitions require giving up what made you successful, not just adding new skills

heuristics.rule: Validate ideas with real people before committing resources, not after
heuristics.condition: When evaluating new product opportunities or strategic bets...
heuristics.action: ...compress the feedback loop by testing early rather than building before validating
heuristics.because: Early validation can reduce development time from six months to two weeks by eliminating work on ideas that would have failed anyway

heuristics.rule: Study who actually gets promoted, not what the rubric says
heuristics.condition: When trying to understand what your org rewards...
heuristics.action: ...pattern-match on recent promotions: who got promoted, what did they work on, what's the narrative about them
heuristics.because: What organizations say they reward and what they actually reward are often different — the promotion record is ground truth

heuristics.rule: Orient day-to-day decisions against a five-year future vision rather than the next promotion cycle
heuristics.condition: When deciding which projects to take, which relationships to build, or which skills to develop
heuristics.action: Ask what the five-year future looks like and work backward to identify what skills, scope, decisions, and relationships are required
heuristics.because: Short-term promotion focus optimizes for the next six months; long-term vision changes the texture of daily decisions and produces compounding career capital

heuristics.rule: Test whether a lateral is actually a promotion by imagining the next hiring manager's reaction
heuristics.condition: When unsure whether a same-title move is a real step up...
heuristics.action: ...ask 'Would a hiring manager at my next target company look at this new title and comp and consider me a more qualified candidate?'
heuristics.because: Career moves only compound if each step makes the next step easier; a move that doesn't improve external perception isn't advancing the career trajectory

heuristics.rule: Match risk tolerance to life stage, not to abstract career ambition.
heuristics.condition: When assessing whether startup risk is appropriate for your situation...
heuristics.action: ...inventory your financial obligations (mortgage, dependents) before treating startup equity as a viable wealth-building strategy
heuristics.because: Startup runway failure with a mortgage and family creates real financial exposure — rational risk calibration means taking more risk when you can absorb downside, not when you most want upside

heuristics.rule: The real cost of an MBA is two years of not compounding your execution track record
heuristics.condition: When considering an MBA to accelerate a PM career
heuristics.action: Compare the MBA path against two years at a great company building craft; only pursue MBA if it provides network, legitimacy signal, or domain access you can't get otherwise
heuristics.because: Internal advocacy and execution track record — not an MBA — drive promotion to Group PM or Director at tech companies

heuristics.rule: Ask for promotion directly and explicitly
heuristics.condition: When you believe you're ready for promotion...
heuristics.action: ...have an explicit conversation with your manager about timing rather than assuming they are tracking or prioritizing it
heuristics.because: Managers often don't prioritize a report's promotion without a direct signal of urgency — silence is interpreted as contentment

heuristics.rule: Look outward at the market rather than only inward at your own product
heuristics.condition: When trying to learn and develop as a PM while operating in a busy role
heuristics.action: Conduct product takedowns of competitors, engage directly with user feedback channels, and analyze decisions made by other product teams
heuristics.because: Internal-focused PMs improve incrementally from their own experiments; external-focused PMs learn from the entire market's experiments simultaneously

heuristics.rule: Switch companies only after you've absorbed the lessons of your current environment
heuristics.condition: When considering leaving before fully extracting value from a role
heuristics.action: Delay the switch until you can clearly articulate what you learned; if you're running from hard feedback, fix the feedback first
heuristics.because: Problems travel with you; switching before learning means you'll face the same issues without the context you had before

heuristics.rule: Diagnose whether your block is a skill gap or a structural constraint before acting
heuristics.condition: When you feel stalled in your promotion trajectory...
heuristics.action: ...determine whether the blocker is performance-based or structural (headcount frozen, budget cycle, tenure requirements) before deciding your response
heuristics.because: The correct action for a skill gap is development; the correct action for a structural constraint is either patience or exit — conflating them wastes time

heuristics.rule: Find two people 5 years ahead of you — one who stayed, one who left — and ask what they'd change
heuristics.condition: When calibrating a stay-vs-leave decision
heuristics.action: Use the pattern of their regrets as your primary data point over salary benchmarks
heuristics.because: Regret patterns from people ahead of you reveal trajectory consequences that present-moment thinking systematically misses

heuristics.rule: If nominal ownership is offered without the authority to say no, it's worse than no ownership
heuristics.condition: When evaluating how much real ownership a new role provides
heuristics.action: Ask specifically about the last two decisions the PM made independently, what happened when they were wrong, and what they pushed back on and won
heuristics.because: Nominal ownership trains you to feel responsible without the authority to act — a habit that is actively harmful to career development

heuristics.rule: State PGWP status explicitly and proactively in resume and interview intro to eliminate employer confusion

I can work for any Canadian employer without any employer-specific authorization. You do not need to sponsor me or file any applications. I am pursuing PR independently.'

heuristics._source: zhihu_互联网人跳槽的注意事项有哪些.txt

heuristics.rule: In the 1–10 phase (3–5 years), go deep in one business domain rather than staying generalist
heuristics.condition: When a PM has passed the early growth stage and is deciding what to specialize in...
heuristics.action: Pick a business domain and accumulate domain-specific know-how, becoming the go-to person in that vertical
heuristics.because: The top answer states that at this stage, proximity to the business becomes the primary differentiator — generalists lose to domain specialists in mid-career competition
heuristics._source: zhihu_产品经理应该如何进行职业规划.txt

heuristics.rule: Don't jump companies or functions if you haven't stayed in one vertical long enough to develop domain depth
heuristics.condition: When a PM considers switching industries or functions after a few years without deep domain expertise in any one area
heuristics.action: Resist the urge to keep switching; pick a vertical and go deep
heuristics.because: Post explicitly warns: 'If a PM has worked many years and has not gone deep in any one industry, that situation is dangerous' — domain expertise compounds and is a core differentiator for senior roles
heuristics._source: zhihu_产品经理的职业生涯规划是怎么样的.txt

heuristics.rule: Establish professional depth before pursuing breadth across industries
heuristics.condition: When a PM is considering whether to switch industries or deepen expertise in a current domain...
heuristics.action: Build strong professional foundations in one domain first before attempting cross-industry moves
heuristics.because: Multiple answers argue that without solid professional grounding, cross-industry moves lead to inability to transfer skills quickly and create decision errors

heuristics.rule: Pick a domain and go deep rather than rotating across industries
heuristics.condition: When a PM is considering switching industries frequently to gain breadth...
heuristics.action: Choose one direction aligned with strengths and interests, and deepen expertise in that domain
heuristics.because: Commenter states that frequent cross-industry job hopping prevents reaching expert-level depth; domain specialization is the only path to becoming a recognized expert
heuristics._source: zhihu_那些35岁以上的产品经理都去做什么了.txt

heuristics.rule: Prioritize LinkedIn and referrals over job boards in the Canadian market
heuristics.condition: When conducting a tech job search in Canada...
heuristics.action: Invest disproportionately in network-based outreach and LinkedIn presence over broad job board applications
heuristics.because: Canada's tech market is smaller than the US, making relationship-based hiring even more pronounced than it already is elsewhere

heuristics.rule: Clarify what a company means by 'no sponsorship' before self-eliminating
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter or job posting says 'no sponsorship' and you are on STEM OPT or OPT...
heuristics.action: Ask explicitly whether they mean no H-1B or no work authorization assistance of any kind — STEM OPT extension forms are a separate, lighter ask
heuristics.because: Multiple commenters (198 and 176 upvotes) report that 'no sponsorship' often means no H-1B petition but companies will still complete STEM OPT I-983 forms, and recruiters themselves conflate the two

heuristics.rule: Keep cold emails under 100 words
heuristics.condition: When drafting any cold outreach email...
heuristics.action: Edit ruthlessly to stay under 100 words; anything over 150 gets skimmed or ignored
heuristics.because: Stated by OP and corroborated by no contradicting comments; reflects attention economy reality of busy hiring managers

heuristics.rule: Clarify the new team's expectations in the first weeks of joining, not after problems arise
heuristics.condition: When onboarding at a new company
heuristics.action: Proactively ask your manager and peers what success looks like at every level — from weekly deliverables to your long-term role
heuristics.because: Best-answer author describes leaving a promising role after half a month specifically because he failed to surface team product expectations early enough; mature teams have low tolerance for new hire misalignment
heuristics._source: zhihu_互联网人跳槽的注意事项有哪些.txt

heuristics.rule: Network (圈子) is a force multiplier that most PMs underweight
heuristics.condition: When a PM has strong skills and track record but keeps hitting promotion ceilings...
heuristics.action: Actively build visibility and relationships outside your immediate team
heuristics.because: Promotion panels at large companies like Alibaba and Tencent involve evaluators who don't know you — internal visibility gaps mean strong work goes unrecognized in the critical promotion defense window
heuristics._source: zhihu_产品经理应该如何进行职业规划.txt

heuristics.rule: By 5+ years, if you still lack clarity on your own career direction, treat that as a serious failure signal requiring retrospection
heuristics.condition: When a PM with 5+ years of experience is still asking 'what should I do next' without a self-formed answer
heuristics.action: Stop looking for external frameworks and do a deep personal retrospective — the inability to self-direct at this stage indicates a structural problem
heuristics.because: Post states directly: 'If you are still confused at the 5-year mark, you need to seriously review yourself' — experienced PMs should have developed judgment by this point
heuristics._source: zhihu_产品经理的职业生涯规划是怎么样的.txt

heuristics.rule: Avoid crossing both specialty and industry simultaneously when making career moves
heuristics.condition: When a PM is considering a job change that involves both a new product type and a new industry...
heuristics.action: Anchor one variable — change industry within the same specialty, or change specialty within the same industry, but not both at once
heuristics.because: Each domain has unique know-how requiring substantial practice to master; doing both simultaneously removes all anchoring advantage
heuristics._source: zhihu_产品经理要如何晋升_有哪些晋升路径.txt

heuristics.rule: For 35+ PMs stuck in large companies, the survival playbook splits by ambition level
heuristics.condition: When a senior PM at a large company faces a ceiling and is evaluating options...
heuristics.action: If upward-oriented: push for management track or jump to smaller company as product head. If stability-oriented: find a sustainable low-profile mode and avoid errors.
heuristics.because: Multiple real cases in answer [2] document both patterns — 'old white rabbit' mode and aggressive upward push — as distinct but viable survival strategies at 35+
heuristics._source: zhihu_那些35岁以上的产品经理都去做什么了.txt

heuristics.rule: Start IELTS prep early — before you need the score
heuristics.condition: When planning your post-graduation Express Entry timeline...
heuristics.action: Begin IELTS preparation well before your 1-year CEC eligibility date so scores are ready when you need them
heuristics.because: Strong English scores are a significant CRS input and test preparation takes time; waiting until you're eligible to apply creates unnecessary delays

heuristics.rule: Reference something specific the recipient wrote, said, or published
heuristics.condition: When personalizing a cold email to a hiring manager...
heuristics.action: Cite a specific blog post, talk, or paper and name what resonated; do not use generic flattery
heuristics.because: OP and the template both demonstrate this; specificity signals genuine interest and distinguishes the email from mass outreach

heuristics.rule: If an interviewer focuses only on technical skills and shows no curiosity about who you are as a person, treat it as a signal to decline

heuristics.action: Assess whether the interview is genuinely two-directional; one-sided skill interrogation indicates a team culture problem

heuristics.rule: Build professional path first, then layer on management responsibilities
heuristics.condition: When a PM at the 5-8 year mark is choosing between specialist and management tracks...
heuristics.action: Solidify individual contributor expertise first, because management requires the ability to replicate your own skills in others — which requires having mastered them yourself
heuristics.because: The second and third answers both state this principle explicitly, noting managers who abandon product depth become increasingly narrow as the industry evolves
